summary: Explains how to use DANE TLSA records with applications that use SRV records to name their servers indirectly, which RFC 6698 did not cover. It tells clients which TLSA records to look up.

plainLanguage.summary: Some services point you to a different address. This tells you how to check the security of the place you were sent to.

subtitle: How a client finds and checks TLSA records when it locates a TLS server through SRV records.

tldr.problem: Some application protocols find their servers indirectly through SRV records, so the rules in RFC 6698 for locating TLSA records cannot be applied directly.
tldr.mechanism: The client trusts only DNSSEC-secure SRV and address answers, then looks up TLSA records under the SRV target server's hostname, port and transport protocol, not under the service domain name. Usable secure TLSA records force the client to use TLS and to match them.
tldr.outcome: SRV-based protocols such as IMAP and XMPP can use DANE with a clear procedure for DNS checks, TLS checks and name matching.

facts.label: TLSA lookup name
facts.value: port, transport and SRV target hostname

today: RFC 7673 is a Proposed Standard. The unit metadata lists no RFC that obsoletes or updates it, and it builds on RFC 6698 and RFC 7671.

sections.title: DANE When a Service Is Found Through SRV
sections.content:
The base DANE specification, RFC 6698, uses DNSSEC-secured TLSA records to associate a server's connection endpoint with its TLS certificate. Some protocols locate their servers through SRV records (RFC 2782), so RFC 6698's rules cannot be applied directly. SMTP uses MX records instead and is covered by RFC 7672.

The approach has a few main points:

  • DNSSEC secures the SRV records that map a service, transport and service domain name to target server endpoints.
  • TLSA records are found using the transport protocol, port number and hostname of the target server, not the service domain name.
  • When DNSSEC-validated TLSA records exist for an endpoint, the client always uses TLS, even if cleartext is available.
  • If at least one TLSA record is usable, the server certificate or key must match one of them.

A connection endpoint is a hostname, transport protocol and port number. The service domain name identifies the application service.
sections.plainLanguage: The service name is like a company name, and the SRV record tells you which office to visit. You then check the ID card of that office.

sections.title: The DNS Checks
sections.content:
The client first makes an SRV query. For this specification to apply, the whole chain of returned RRsets, including any CNAME or DNAME aliases, MUST be DNSSEC "secure". If the lookup is "bogus" or fails for reasons other than no records, the client MUST abort. If it is "insecure" or there are no SRV records, this protocol does not apply and the client SHOULD fall back to its non-DNSSEC, non-DANE behavior. Server order and selection still follow SRV priority and weight.

For each target, the client makes A and/or AAAA queries. If a returned RRset is secure, it MUST do a TLSA query. If none are secure, it MUST NOT do a TLSA query. If the address lookup is "bogus" or "indeterminate", it MUST NOT connect to that endpoint and uses the next SRV target, which helps prevent downgrade attacks.

The TLSA query name is built from the port in the SRV data, the transport from the SRV query name and the SRV target hostname as base domain.
sections.plainLanguage: First check that the directions you were given were not tampered with. If they look fake, do not go. If they are real, look up the ID card for the place they point to.

sections.title: From SRV Record to TLSA Query
sections.content:
The RFC gives an IMAP example. The SRV record _imap._tcp.example.com. 86400 IN SRV 10 0 9143 imap.example.net. leads to the TLSA query _9143._tcp.imap.example.net. IN TLSA ?.

The client then checks whether the TLSA records are usable (Section 4.1 of RFC 6698):

  • Secure and usable: the client MUST use TLS and use the records to validate the certificate.
  • Bogus or indeterminate, or a lookup failure other than no records: the client MUST NOT connect to that target, though other SRV targets may be used.
  • Insecure or no TLSA records: the client proceeds as if there were none, and MAY connect with or without TLS per the application protocol or client policy.
sections.plainLanguage: The ID-card lookup uses the name of the office you are visiting, plus the door number and kind of door. Good ID means go in with a secure connection. Suspicious ID means do not go in.

sections.title: The TLS Checks and Name Matching
sections.content:
If the SRV and TLSA responses were secure, the client MUST use TLS. With zero usable TLSA associations, it validates the certificate by normal PKIX rules or protocol-specific rules such as RFC 6125, using the DNSSEC status of the SRV answer. It SHOULD use SNI or its protocol equivalent, and the service domain name is the preferred name.

  • SRV insecure: reference identifiers include the service domain name and MUST NOT include the SRV target hostname.
  • SRV secure: reference identifiers include both the service domain name and the SRV target hostname.

With one or more usable TLSA associations, the client processes them per Section 2.1 of RFC 6698. If the certificate or its public key matches a record with certificate usage DANE-EE, the client MUST ignore the RFC 5280 validation checks and the RFC 6125 reference identifier checks, because the TLSA record supersedes the non-key information in the certificate.

For usages other than DANE-EE, name checks still matter: a PKIX-TA record only authenticates the CA, and third parties can get certificates from the same CA.
sections.plainLanguage: If the ID card names the exact badge, that settles it. If it only names the issuing office, you must also check that the name on the badge is the one you expected.

sections.title: Guidance for Operators, Developers and Protocol Authors
sections.content:
Server operators MUST secure the SRV and A/AAAA records with DNSSEC and SHOULD publish at least one TLSA record. With DANE-EE, the certificate need not contain the service domain name or the target hostname, but relying only on DANE-EE might stop clients that do not support this specification from connecting with TLS. For other usages, the certificate MUST contain an identifier matching the service domain name and/or the target server hostname. Multi-tenant servers can use SNI to choose a certificate.

Application developers may run address and TLSA queries in parallel. A TLSA record can be ignored if its address record turns out not to be secure, so this is not harmful from a security perspective. Internationalized names need to use the A-label form.

Protocol authors are pointed to topics that application-specific documents could cover, including fallback logic, behavior for clients without SRV support, any SNI equivalent, and combined SRV and NAPTR discovery as in SIP. The XMPP DNA draft is cited as an example.
sections.plainLanguage: Shop owners should sign their directions, keep an ID card on file and be ready for visitors asking about different company names. App builders can look things up at the same time to be faster.

sections.title: Mixed Security and Rationale
sections.content:
Not every endpoint for a service domain name must have TLSA records, so partial deployment does not break the service. SRV sorting is not altered to prefer secure endpoints. The RFC states that a site wanting to be secure needs to deploy the protocol completely, and a partial deployment is not secure.

The rationale appendix says the long-term goal is for TLS certificates to verify the target server hostname rather than the service domain name. That is more convenient for servers hosting many domains. The same TLSA records then work both with this specification and with direct connections in the style of RFC 6698, and replacing a certificate needs only one part of the DNS updated. The RFC deliberately gives no option to put TLSA records under the service domain name, because that adds complexity without benefit.

The downside is that clients not completing DNSSEC validation must check the certificate against the service domain name under RFC 6125, so SNI support or its equivalent is needed for backward compatibility.
sections.plainLanguage: It is fine if only some offices have ID cards, but then the whole company is not fully protected. The designers chose to check the office, not the company name, because that is simpler for big hosts.
